title: Writing for agents

story: An early skill for checking work had one line about tests: "YOU MUST ALWAYS RUN ALL THE TESTS BEFORE YOU COMMIT." On Monday, Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, fixed a typo in a button label and ran the whole backend suite first: forty minutes on a full machine, for one changed word in the frontend.

On Tuesday it renamed a field in a serializer, the code that turns database rows into API responses. It ran all the tests again, they passed, and it opened the PR. No test covered the old field name, which the published Python SDK still reads, so the break showed up later, in the SDK. Nova obeyed the rule perfectly both days. It was too much for the typo and too little for the rename, because the rule never said what it was for.
hook.question: How do we write instructions that an agent applies with judgement: light on a typo, careful on a risky change?

read.h: An order without a reason is followed everywhere
p: Current Claude models follow instructions closely, and they react strongly to emphasis. Anthropic's prompting guide warns about exactly this: text written in capitals for older, less attentive models now makes Claude over-apply the rule, and the guide's fix is to "dial back any aggressive language". The same guide shows the other half. "NEVER use ellipses" works less well than saying that the reply will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine that cannot pronounce them, because, in the guide's words, Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation.

That is the whole idea of this lesson. A reader who knows the goal and the reason can handle the case you never wrote down. Compare the two versions of the testing rule below. The first gives an order and no way to judge. The second says what we want to be true, where to start and why that is usually enough, which signs mean go deeper, and what to do when a check fails. It also tells a person what to do, which matters because people and Nova read the same skills.

code.file: the same rule, before and after
code.text:
<!-- Before: an order with no reason -->
YOU MUST ALWAYS RUN ALL THE TESTS BEFORE YOU COMMIT. NEVER SKIP THIS STEP.

<!-- After: a goal, a starting point with its reason, signs, and the failure path -->
Goal: the commit does not break main, and you know which tests prove it.
Start with the tests next to the files you changed and the area's lint and type checks.
That covers most changes in minutes; the whole suite is for code many modules depend on.
Look deeper when you changed shared code, a serializer, a migration or anything the SDK uses.
If a test fails, fix the code rather than the test, because a loosened test hides the next bug too.

notes.text: Capitals tell the reader this matters, but not why, so it cannot tell a typo from a risky change.
The goal, in terms of the result, not the method.
The reason the default is enough, which is also the reason to leave it.
Signs to look deeper: concrete situations, so the reader can recognise them.
The failure path, with its reason, so variations nobody listed are refused too.

read.h: Match the freedom to the risk
p: Not everything should be left to judgement. Anthropic's skill guide calls this the degree of freedom and uses a picture: a narrow bridge with cliffs on both sides has one safe way across, so you give exact steps; an open field has many good paths, so you give a direction and trust the walker. Checking a Django migration is a bridge: there is one right command, ./manage.py makemigrations --dry-run --check, and the skill should say exactly that. Deciding how deeply to check a change is a field: it depends on the change, so the skill gives a starting point and signs.

Our verify skill, the one people, Nova and every routine use before saying a change is done, is built this way. Where to start names exact commands, through a short reference file per area. Signs to look deeper names the situations that need more. Prove a check can fail turns a vague habit into one concrete action: break your own change on purpose and watch the check catch it. When a check fails closes the cheap path and says why. Rules that must never break, such as never editing the tests you are judged by, are not written as prose at all; a hook and a required check enforce them, and the skill only explains them, so nobody is surprised.

code.text:
# verify: proof, not claims

Goal: a reviewer can see that each check ran and could have failed, without running it themselves.

## Where to start
Run the area's verify command (references/per-area.md). Then check what the user would see.

## Signs to look deeper
You changed a serializer, a migration, a proto, a public SDK function or shared UI; there is no test near
the diff; the change is about timing, permissions or time zones.

## Prove a check can fail
Plant a small bug in your change (flip a condition), run the check, watch it fail, revert. If it still
passes, the check does not cover your change: write a better one.

## When a check fails
It is yours until main's latest run shows the same failure; then link that run. Fix the code rather than
the check, because a loosened check hides the next bug too. If you think a test is wrong, say why in the PR.

notes.text: The title says the goal in a few words.
The goal in terms of the reviewer: what should be true when the work is done.
The bridge part: exact commands, kept in a reference file so this page stays short.
The field part: signs, not a checklist per file type, so the reader can judge new cases.
One concrete action that proves a check covers the change.
The cheap path, named and closed, with the reason in the same sentence.

deeper.h: Go deeper: when a fixed shape is the point
p: Sometimes the reader needs the same shape every time, and then a strict template is the right low-freedom choice. pr-story, the skill for pull request descriptions, fixes the headings and their order: What changes, Why, How it was checked, What was not checked and why, Risk and rollback, Where to look first. A reviewer from another team then knows where the proof sits on any PR, written by a person or by Nova, and fcp's PR template uses the same headings so there is only one.

The checking guide, a reference page inside verify, is the opposite: for each kind of change, from docs to a dependency bump, a place to start, the signs to look deeper, and the proof that fits. It names only commands that exist today and says plainly which planned tools are not there yet, because a guide that sends the reader to a missing command sends it into a wall.

A skill shares the context window with everything else Claude is doing, so every line has to earn its place. The skill guide's default assumption is that Claude is already very smart: only write what it cannot know, such as our commands, our risky areas and our reasons. Point to code by path instead of pasting it, because a pasted serializer is wrong the day someone changes the file, while a path is read fresh every time. Keep deeper files one link away from SKILL.md, use one word for one thing throughout, and avoid sentences tied to a date, such as "until the end of November", which become false without anyone noticing.

Then test the text, because a sentence that reads well can still make results worse. The evals from the previous lesson answer that: a rule earns its place when the scores are lower without it. That gives a simple habit called a rule diet. Once a month, each skill's owner removes one rule, runs the evals with and without it, and keeps the removal if the scores hold. Skills get shorter over time instead of longer, and each rule that stays has a measured reason.

lab.title: Check a skill's voice, then rewrite a loud one
needs: python3 (it comes with Apple's command line tools)
lab.goal: Run a small checker that catches what a script can see in a skill, rewrite a loud skill into a goal, a reason and signs, and then find the problems no script can see.

guess.q: A skill for planning says "IMPORTANT: ALWAYS ask the requester questions before planning." What will a current Claude model most likely do on a one-line typo ticket?

options.text: Skip the questions, because the ticket is obviously clear
options.why: The rule says ALWAYS and gives no reason, so the model has nothing that tells it a clear ticket is an exception.

options.text: Ask the requester questions anyway, and the small ticket waits for answers nobody needed
options.why: Current models follow emphatic rules closely, so the rule is applied where it does not fit. A reason and signs ("ask when two readings lead to different code") would let it skip the questions.

options.text: Ignore the skill completely, because capitals are filtered out
options.why: Nothing filters capitals. If anything, emphasis makes the rule weigh more.

follow.say: Make a lab folder with two skills: the loud one from the story, and verify written in the calm voice, with the reference file it points to.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p12-4/skills/run-tests ~/academy-labs/p12-4/skills/verify/references && cd ~/academy-labs/p12-4
cat > skills/run-tests/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: run-tests
description: "Testing skill."
---
# run-tests

YOU MUST ALWAYS RUN ALL THE TESTS BEFORE YOU COMMIT. NEVER SKIP THIS STEP.
IMPORTANT: DO NOT DELETE TESTS.
EOF
cat > skills/verify/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: verify
description: "Use before saying a code change is done: choose checks that prove it works, run the area's verify command, show a new check can fail by planting a bug, and record proof a reviewer can see."
when_to_use: "After editing code, tests or config; when a check fails and you need to know whether it is yours."
---
# verify: proof, not claims

Goal: a reviewer can see that each check ran and could have failed, without running it themselves.

## Where to start
Run the area's verify command (references/per-area.md). Then check what the user would see.

## Signs to look deeper
You changed a serializer, a migration, a proto, a public SDK function or shared UI; there is no test near
the diff; the change is about timing, permissions or time zones.

## Prove a check can fail
Plant a small bug in your change (flip a condition), run the check, watch it fail, revert. If it still
passes, the check does not cover your change: write a better one.

## When a check fails
It is yours until main's latest run shows the same failure; then link that run. Fix the code rather than
the check, because a loosened check hides the next bug too. If you think a test is wrong, say why in the PR.
EOF
cat > skills/verify/references/per-area.md <<'EOF'
# Verify commands per area
- frontend/: npm run lint, npm run check-types, then the related vitest files
- cloud/: ./scripts/local_run_backend_unit_tests.sh cloud <module path>
EOF

follow.say: Write the checker. It is a small version of the checks our plugin CI runs on every skill: the name matches the folder, the description says when to use the skill and is not too long, loud words get a warning, and every references/ link points at a real file.
Run it on both skills. Errors fail the check; warnings are for a person to judge.
follow.do:

follow.say: Pointing to a file instead of pasting it only works while the file exists. Rename the reference file, the way a refactor would, and run the checker on verify again. Then rename it back.

python3 check_skill.py skills/verify/SKILL.md; echo "exit $?"
mv skills/verify/references/commands.md skills/verify/references/per-area.md

ERROR skills/verify/SKILL.md: body line 6: references/per-area.md does not exist

lab.build: Rewrite skills/run-tests/SKILL.md in the calm voice. Give it a description that says what it does and starts with "Use before" or "Use when", a when_to_use line with the situations people are in, and a body with a goal, a default starting point with its reason, signs to look deeper, and the failure path with its reason. No capitals for emphasis. Run python3 check_skill.py skills/run-tests/SKILL.md until it prints ok and exit 0. Then read your text as Nova on two tickets, a typo in a button label and a renamed serializer field, and check that it leads to a light check on the first and a careful one on the second.
checks: The checker prints ok and exit 0 for verify and for your rewritten run-tests
Your description says what the skill does and when to use it, in words a person would type
Every instruction in your body has a reason in the same or the next sentence
Your body names at least two concrete signs to look deeper
Renaming per-area.md made the checker fail with a dead-link error, and you renamed it back

solution.text:
---
name: run-tests
description: "Use before you commit a code change: pick the tests that cover it, run them, and show they can fail, so the commit does not break main."
when_to_use: "About to commit or push; a test failed and you are not sure it is yours."
---
# run-tests

Goal: the commit does not break main, and you know which tests prove it.

Start with the tests next to the files you changed and the area's lint and type checks. That covers
most changes in minutes; the whole suite is for changes that many modules depend on.

Look deeper when you changed shared code, a serializer, a migration or anything the SDK uses: run the
wider suite, because a break there shows up far from your diff.

If a test fails, fix the code rather than the test, because a deleted or loosened test hides the next
bug too. If you think the test itself is wrong, say why in the PR and let the reviewer decide.

lab.fix:
A teammate wrote skills/check-api/SKILL.md, and the checker says ok. It still has three problems no script catches: a sentence tied to a date ("Until the end of November, run the old schema check"), a pointer that sends the reader to a wiki page which links to yet another page, and a pasted serializer that will be wrong the day someone changes the real file. Save it, run the checker to see ok, then rewrite it: describe the condition instead of the date, point to one reference file in the skill's own folder, and replace the pasted code with the path of the real file.

---
name: check-api
description: "Use when a change touches a cloud API endpoint: check the response shape and the SDK that calls it."
---
# check-api

Goal: an API change never breaks the published SDK or the dashboard.

Until the end of November, run the old schema check, because the new one is not merged yet.
For the details of each endpoint, read the notes in the cloud wiki, which link to the field list.

The current serializer looks like this, so compare your change with it:

    class DatasetSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
        class Meta:
            fields = ["uid", "name", "created_at"]
explain: Why did the loud rule make Nova do too much on the typo and too little on the serializer rename?
When should a skill give an exact command, and when should it give signs and leave the choice to the reader?
What can the checker catch, what can only a person reading the skill catch, and what can only the evals catch?
lab.done: The checker passes for verify and your rewritten run-tests, and your fixed check-api has no date, no second-hand pointer and no pasted code.

check.q: A skill says "CRITICAL: You MUST use the kb tool for every question." Since a model upgrade, Nova searches the brain even for "rename this variable". What is the best fix?

options.text: Add "except for trivial tasks" in capitals
options.why: Another loud rule with no reason. Nova still cannot tell which tasks count as trivial.

options.text: Say when the tool helps and why: "Search the brain when the task depends on how our systems work, because those answers are not in the code."
options.why: Normal wording with a reason lets the model decide case by case. Anthropic's guide gives this exact fix for tools that over-trigger after an upgrade.

options.text: Remove the kb tool from Nova
options.why: The tool is useful. The problem is the instruction, not the tool.

check.q: Which part of a skill should be exact steps rather than signs and judgement?

options.text: How deeply to check a change
options.why: That depends on the change. Signs to look deeper serve it better than a fixed list.

options.text: Which edge cases a plan should name
options.why: That depends on the ticket. Examples and signs help more than a fixed list.

options.text: A fragile operation with one right way, such as the exact migration check command
options.why: A narrow bridge: one safe path and a costly mistake, so the skill gives the exact command.

check.q: In this month's rule diet, an owner removes a rule from verify and the evals still score the same, with and without the plugin. What happens?

options.text: The removal is kept: the rule cost attention on every run without improving results
options.why: A rule earns its place only when results are worse without it. Shorter skills leave more room for the task.

options.text: The rule goes back, because more rules are safer
options.why: Every line costs context on every run. A rule that changes nothing is a cost with no benefit.

options.text: The rule is moved into capitals so it is noticed more
options.why: If removing it changes nothing, louder text only adds the risk of over-applying it.

p: A style guide, STYLE.md in RhinoHealth/claude-plugins, sets the voice for every shared skill and CLAUDE.md file: the first line says when to use the skill; the body has goals, reasons, examples and signs to look deeper in calm words, with no capitals for emphasis; walls live in hooks and infrastructure, not prompts; a CLI is preferred to an MCP server; an agent gets 5 to 10 skills; SKILL.md stays short with references/ for depth; evals come before long instructions. catalog.yaml names every shared skill's plugin and owner, and plugin CI fails a pull request that adds a skill missing from it or with fewer than 3 eval cases, and warns on capitalised MUST, NEVER or CRITICAL.

The rhino-core skills are written in this voice: plan-and-grill (ask first or plan now, then a one-screen plan), verify with its checking guide, and pr-story with the fixed headings that fcp's PR template now shares. fcp's frontend/AGENTS.md and root CLAUDE.md point to verify in one line. On the first Monday of each month, each owner opens a rule-diet pull request, and the results go to the monthly run review.

tickets.why: STYLE.md, catalog.yaml with owners, and the monthly rule diet.
verify: where to start, signs to look deeper, plant a bug, honest failures and recorded proof.
The checking guide: start, look deeper and proof per kind of change, with commands that exist today.
pr-story: fixed headings for a reviewer from another team, folded into fcp's PR template.
plan-and-grill, written in this voice, with evals for when to ask and when to plan.

words.plain: Concrete situations named in a skill that tell the reader the default check is not enough this time.
How much a skill leaves to judgement: exact steps for a fragile task, a goal and signs for a task with many good paths.
What the skill says to do when a check fails, with the reason, so the cheap way out is closed.
A monthly pull request that removes one rule from a skill and keeps the removal if the evals still hold.

review.q: Rewrite "NEVER deploy on Fridays" for a skill, in the calm voice.
review.a: Something like: "Prefer to deploy early in the week, because fewer people are around to watch a Friday release. If it must go out on Friday, name who watches it." A goal, the reason, and what to do in the exception.

review.q: Name three things a script can check in a skill and two only a person can.
review.a: Script: name matches the folder, the description says when, links point to real files, loud words. Person: whether every rule has a reason, whether a sentence will go stale, whether the signs are concrete.

review.q: Why do walls such as "never edit the tests you are judged by" not live in a skill?
review.a: Text is guidance a model can misread or be talked out of. A hook and a required check enforce the wall whatever the model believes; the skill only explains it.

remember: Write the goal, the reason and the signs to look deeper in calm words, give exact steps only where there is one safe way, leave walls to code, and let the evals decide which rules stay.
